arcade_cabinet.real_object: In this world there is no arcade: each cabinet is a 1912-1924 Vantry-descended coin-operated receiving cabinet, i.e. a second-hand floor-standing radio-receiver console in Bakelite and brass with a circular long-persistence cathode-ray scope where a loudspeaker grille would be, a valve rack behind a hinged service door, wet cells in the base and an enamel-on-steel programme card in a lit frame above the glass; the nearest real 1927-1928 objects are the Atwater Kent / RCA Radiola floor console, the Mills / Caille / Mutoscope penny-arcade upright, and a laboratory oscillograph or 1928 mechanical televisor for the scope itself.
arcade_cabinet.period_note: Present is 1928 (bible VIII.5.h); the chassis plates read 1912, 1916, 1919, 1922, 1924 or are blank, so every machine predates the reopening and Vantry & Co. stopped servicing anything in 1924. Rule of Signal (brief section 2, bible VIII.2): the scope, valves and receiver are forty years early (a CRT picture in a 1927 case), but the carcass is ordinary 1927-or-older second-hand furniture under VIII.4 - dark phenolic Bakelite, dull brass, oak, cloth-braided flex, glass valves, nickel guards, copper contacts; no aluminium, no stainless, no chrome, no injection-moulded colour. The Blender assembly's four 1980s arcade silhouettes (its docstring literally says 'late-80s shape with fins', bodies metal / fabric_cool / chrome / enamel) were written before ruling VIII.5.g of 2026-08-09 and now contradict it; the F01 lobby and common-room copies were already removed for reading 'later than 1928'.

bar_signage.display_name: Harukiya frontage sign (kanji board, chochin lantern, bulb arrow)
bar_signage.real_object: The street sign of a Japanese-run basement bar on a Queens block in late 1928: a hand-painted timber fascia signboard (kanban) reading 春木屋 lit from outside by two gooseneck reflector lamps, a red bamboo-and-washi chochin lantern (akachochin, the izakaya open-for-business signal) hung on a bracket arm, and an incandescent light-bulb arrow sign pointing down the enclosed stair to a below-grade entrance.
bar_signage.period_note: Present is late 1928. Under Bible VIII.2 (Rule of Signal) a painted board, incandescent trough lights, a paper lantern and a bulb arrow carry no signal, so they are 1928 or older, second-hand and worn; the ledger dates the bar from the building's 1912 first life through the 1927 partial demolition to the 1928 reopening, so the board has sixteen years of weather on it. All three technologies are period-correct pre-neon shopfront conventions (bulb-studded electric signs c.1900-1925; gooseneck reflector sign lighting on painted fascias; the akachochin has marked izakaya since Edo). The romaji line says KARAOKE: karaoke is ruled a signal machine, native under VIII.2 and the ledger's NYC ADAPTATION entry, so it is licensed, not an anachronism. Tube neon existed in the US from 1923 but the script deliberately avoids it, consistent with Accord 9. One thing no design document addresses: Prohibition (1920-1933). A lit sign reading BAR on a Queens street in 1928 is historically a speakeasy-era impossibility (real ones read cafe, restaurant, chop suey or nothing); this is unruled, so flag it under brief §9 rather than correct it.

bodega_signage.display_name: Bodega shop sign (HALF BAKED, Deli & Grocery)
bodega_signage.real_object: The street signage of a 1927-1928 corner grocery-delicatessen across from a Queens walk-up: a hand-painted wooden fascia signboard, a canvas roll-up awning with the name painted on its scalloped valance, a sheet-metal or porcelain-enamel projecting sign on an iron bracket (at most an incandescent-bulb electric sign with opal-glass letters), gold-leaf window and transom lettering, and supplier enamel signs nailed round the door; never a backlit vinyl valance, an acrylic lightbox or a fluorescent tube.
bodega_signage.period_note: The present is late 1928 (bible VIII.2 says 1927; the brief says late 1928). A shop sign does not carry, capture, switch, store or reproduce a signal, so under the Rule of Signal it is 1928-or-older and probably second-hand, and VIII.6 says the divergence licenses no other anachronism. The script's stated vocabulary is wrong by decades: fluorescent tubes were introduced commercially in 1938, acrylic sheet (Plexiglas/Lucite) in 1933-36, and the backlit vinyl awning valance is a 1970s-80s convention; even tube neon, which the header rightly avoids, was a 1923-onward luxury a corner grocery would not have bought. A 1928 Queens grocer advertised with sign-writer's paint and gold leaf on a wooden fascia, a striped cotton-duck awning on a pipe frame, a porcelain-enamel or tin projecting sign on a wrought-iron bracket, and if electric at all, exposed tungsten bulbs or an opal-glass box lit from inside by bulbs, with gooseneck reflector lamps throwing light onto the board from outside (the same pre-neon convention the Harukiya sign already uses). Twenty-four-hour operation is fixed by the fiction (night clerk, 03:30 visits) and period New York did have all-night delicatessens and lunch rooms; the period phrasing was OPEN ALL NIGHT or OPEN DAY AND NIGHT rather than OPEN 24 HOURS.

Backlit vinyl, acrylic lightbox and fluorescent tube therefore fall outside canon regardless of the header's 'iconic NYC vocabulary' argument.

The bodega must not be more lit than the bar.

boiler.display_name: Boiler — 1912 hand-fired sectional coal steam boiler
boiler.real_object: The Orison's original 1912 heating plant: a coal-fired, hand-stoked cast-iron sectional low-pressure steam boiler of the American Radiator Company 'Ideal' class, lagged and patched by sixteen years of caretakers, feeding twenty-three one-pipe steam radiators from a basement plant room.
boiler.period_note: The present is late 1928 and the plant is the building's 1912 original, so it is a sixteen-year-old anthracite boiler, not a new one; cast-iron sectional boilers of the Ideal / Arco class were the standard apartment-house steam plant from the 1890s through the 1920s. It carries no signal, so under the bible's §VIII divergence rule it is strictly 1928-or-older hardware: no oil burner, no automatic stoker, no electric control. The Hartford loop (introduced 1919) and a check damper in the breeching are exactly the kind of later fitter's additions the script header licenses ('every caretaker merely added another clamp, valve or instruction tag').

darts.real_object: A heavy bar tumbler or nonic pint glass, chipped at the rim, standing on a shelf beside the throwing line of a 1928 bar and holding three mismatched house darts (turned-wood or brass barrels, steel points, turkey-feather flights) for the elm or clay dartboard hung on the wall 2.37 m away.
darts.period_note: This prop is not in a rented flat: it sits in F01_BAR, the Harukiya, the Japanese-named ground-floor bar (docs/harukiya_reference_notes.md files the bar as a film transplant with retrofits re-dated to 1928 by amendment A0.5; its ledger never files the darts at all). Darts is an English pub game; in 1927-28 America it existed as an immigrant pub import and as Philadelphia/eastern-Pennsylvania 'American darts' (Widdy Company wooden darts with turkey-feather flights on a basswood board). English boards of the twenties were elm or poplar 'log-end' boards soaked overnight to stop cracking, or the Nodor modelling-clay board (Ted Leggatt, c.1923); the sisal bristle board arrived in 1935 and is too late, so gen_layout's 'sisal face' comment is a mild anachronism the references should not reinforce. Cheap house darts were turned wood with lead weighting and feather flights; knurled brass barrels on cane shafts existed but were the dearer option. The bulged 'nonic' tumbler is period-correct and American (Hugo Pick, Albert Pick & Co., Chicago, US patent 1913). The 1.73 m bull and 2.37 m oche in gen_layout are the 1977 BDO/WDF standard; 1920s throw lines were commonly 8-9 ft and varied by house, but that is layout geometry, not this prop's. The repo holds no ruling on Prohibition (1920-33) for the Harukiya, so treat the glass as bar glassware without resolving what it held. Divergence rule: nothing here carries a signal, so everything is 1928 or older, cheap, second-hand and a bit broken.

fridge.period_note: The present is late 1928 in an alternate timeline where only signal technology diverged. neon_sign.real_object: A late-1920s American 'electric sign' in its two trade forms: a double-faced projecting blade of painted sheet steel on an angle-iron frame, hung off the facade on wall brackets with tie rods and edged with an exposed incandescent bulb border, or a flat sheet-steel fascia pan; in either case carrying bent clear-glass luminous tubing (red-orange neon or blue argon-mercury) mounted proud of the dark face on glass tube supports and fed by a luminous-tube transformer in a ventilated steel box via rigid conduit.
neon_sign.period_note: Neon tube signage reached US commercial use in 1923 (R008, NPS dossier) and was franchised in New York through Claude Neon Lights from about 1924-25, so in late 1928 neon is the newest and dearest kind of electric sign in the city, seen on theatres, hotels and chain drugstores rather than modest walk-ups. The honest reading for a 1912 Vantry showcase building is an older bulb-bordered projecting electric sign whose letters were re-done in neon around 1927-28, which is exactly the neon-plus-chaser-bulb combination the script already claims. Under the bible's Rule of Signal a lit sign carries no signal, so it gets no forty-year advance: 1928 tubing is clear lead glass with red-orange neon or blue argon-mercury only; phosphor-coated pink, white and pastel tubes are a 1933+ development, so the default pink tint and the script's 'phosphor coat' dead-tube note read later than the setting (the DRUGS cyan is close to period argon-mercury blue; an amber stage sign in 1928 would be neon in yellow-tinted glass). shop_sign.display_name: Shop sign — fascia name, trade line and projecting blade
shop_sign.real_object: The signwriter's hand-painted lettering of a 1927-28 Queens neighbourhood shop parade: the shop name in large capitals with a smaller trade line beneath it on the painted wood fascia board between transom and cornice, one word repeated on both faces of a projecting blade sign hung square to the wall on an iron bracket, and, where the shop had a roll-up canvas awning, the name painted on the awning valance instead of the hidden fascia.
shop_sign.period_note: Through the 1920s the ordinary American shop sign was still a sign painter's job — oil-paint block, Egyptian or Clarendon capitals, shaded or keylined, sometimes gilded on the prosperous fronts (druggist, funeral, pawn) — laid on a painted plank fascia in the band above the transom, with porcelain-enamel brand signs and double-faced sheet-metal blade signs on wrought-iron brackets for the long view up the street; roll-up cotton-duck awnings with the name lettered on the scalloped valance were standard on sunny frontages. Bulb-outlined electric signs belonged to theatres and department stores, and neon (in New York from c.1924-25) was still a novelty, so a side-street parade in late 1928 is painted, and lit only by the shop's own door lamp — which is also what the Rule of Signal demands, since a painted sign carries no signal and stays 1928-or-older. Berenice Abbott's and Walker Evans's 1930s storefront photographs are a few years late but record exactly this 1920s vocabulary surviving in place.

songbook_terminal.real_object: An 1857-1860s Paris phonautograph as sold by Rudolph Koenig: a horn (Scott's 1857 prototype used a wooden barrel; Koenig's commercial version a large plaster-of-Paris horn) feeding a membrane diaphragm whose hog-bristle stylus scratches a trace into lampblacked paper wrapped on a hand-cranked brass cylinder that advances on a lead screw — a sound-writing laboratory instrument that records and cannot play back, standing here as a ~70-year-old second-hand machine on a wooden plinth at chest height by the bar's stage.
songbook_terminal.period_note: Patented in Paris in March 1857 by Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville (a printer and bookseller), manufactured and sold from c.1859 by the acoustic-instrument maker Rudolph Koenig and listed in Koenig's apparatus catalogue; Scott's 1860 phonautograms were not heard until First Sounds optically reconstructed them in 2008. In the late-1928 Harukiya it is an old, unelectrified French laboratory instrument, older than the building, so reference material belongs to 1857-1870s Paris acoustic apparatus and to the museum survivors (Smithsonian NMAH, Science Museum London, Musée des arts et métiers), not to anything of the 1920s; the bible's III.2 rules this object explicitly, so the Rule of Signal is not to be re-applied to it. Two data leftovers from the superseded karaoke box remain in the tree and are not evidence: the marker's "network": "electrical" in building_layout.json and the "rented karaoke box" comment in art/data/gen_layout.py.

speaker.period_note: This prop reproduces a signal, so bible VIII.2 (the Rule of Signal) moves it forty years forward: the fiction-correct silhouette is a late-1960s moving-coil studio monitor or bookshelf loudspeaker, and the script's choice (veneer box, cone woofer, horn tweeter, port) is right in class. VIII.4 then fixes the materials: walnut or mahogany veneer on plywood, paper cone with pleated-paper or treated-cloth surround, a phenolic/Bakelite horn flare, brass fittings, cloth-braided flex and screw terminals, no aluminium, no stainless, no foam surround and no injection-moulded colour; Accord 9 makes it twenty years old and repaired by four people, which is why the header says salvage grade. street_lamp.real_object: A 1928 Queens street was lit by cast-iron city standards with incandescent luminaires: the bishop's-crook (NYC Type 24), the Corvington (Type 1BC) or the straight Type 6 mast-arm post, each hanging an opal or Holophane prismatic globe under a spun-metal reflector cap and burning a clear tungsten series lamp; there was no sodium light (first installations 1932 in the Netherlands, mid-1930s in the USA) and no cobra head (1957).
street_lamp.period_note: The generator authors these as 'sodium heads at 2000 K' and the script as a cobra head, both about thirty years ahead of the setting; a street lamp carries no signal, so the Rule of Signal does not license it. Nothing in the notes or brief rules on it (the driving-rain sky proposal's 'sodium city glow' is a proposal, not a ruling), so this is a question for the owner. The period answer is a tungsten-warm opal or prismatic globe on a bishop's crook, which keeps 'warmest thing outside' as a colour cue without the anachronism; the incandescent street-series lamp was itself warm and dim.

vantry_point.real_object: A fictional but historically grounded 1912 hard-wired ceiling listening head: a carbon-granule telephone-transmitter capsule behind a brass grille in a moulded phenolic (Bakelite-type) saucer, on the Orison's dedicated house fire/flood/line-test signal circuit, standing in for the modern smoke detector that does not exist in this world.
vantry_point.period_note: The Orison present is late 1928; the point was installed with the 1912 fabric and has sixteen years of ceiling paint and failed plaster around it. Under the Divergence rule (bible VIII.2) its signal function is forty years early, but its body is strictly 1912 materials: moulded phenolic (Bakelite, patented 1907-09), dull brass, cloth-and-copper wire and an enamelled mechanical flag. Its real-world anchors are the carbon telephone transmitter (Berliner 1897, Western Electric solid-back and 1927 perforated mountings), Gamewell alarm-telegraph apparatus (1909) and the Dictograph-era concealed room transmitter. No real 1927 Queens walk-up had a domestic smoke detector; commercial buildings at most had thermostatic alarm-telegraph circuits.
